podcast.title: "Oh No" During "You Really Got Me" Solo
podcast.body: During the second, successful take of the "You Really Got Me" re-recording session, Ray Davis "yelled, oh no, with excitement" as Dave Davis launched into his iconic guitar solo. Ray initially believed he had distracted Dave at this crucial moment, but Dave instead "smirked and delivered live the defining solos of the rock genre." "Going into the solo, Ray yelled, oh no, with excitement, looking over at Dave, and became convinced that he'd distracted Dave at the crucial moment."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Advice from Alexis Korner
podcast.body: Following a gig at the art college where Alexis Korner performed with The Rolling Stones as support, Ray Davis approached Korner for advice on advancing his music career. Korner recommended he speak with Giorgio Gomelsky, a promoter and manager known for organizing many of the Stones' early performances. "Davis went up to Conor and asked him for advice about moving on in the music world."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Big Bill Broonzy Influence & Working-Class Identity
podcast.body: A 16-minute documentary about Big Bill Broonzy's tour of Belgium, "Low Light and Blue Smoke," deeply affected Ray. His father's approval of Broonzy, describing him as a "real man" unlike "high-voiced girly-sounding pop singers," resonated with Ray's respect for older generations' musical tastes. Crucially, Ray felt Broonzy's performance sounded "authentic" and "working class," which aligned with Ray's own working-class background, distinguishing him from "comparatively privileged" contemporaries like John Lennon or Mick Jagger. "He said later that he thought that Boonsy sounded like him, even though Boonsy was black and American, he sounded working class, and unlike many of his contemporaries, Ray Davis did have a working class background."

podcast.title: Brian Epstein's Solo Interest
podcast.body: During a rehearsal of The Bull Weevils (an early incarnation of The Kinks), Brian Epstein, manager of The Beatles, attended. He expressed "vague" interest in signing Ray as a solo artist but showed no interest in the group itself. This was considered "odd" as Ray was not performing solo leads at the time, with Robert Wace and Dave Davis handling most vocals. "Epstein said he was vaguely interested in sounding Ray as a solo artist, but didn't want the group, and nothing further came of it."

podcast.title: Career Expectations & Segovia Ambition
podcast.body: Upon quitting art school to pursue music full-time, Ray Davis initially harbored modest expectations for his pop star career. He hoped that six months as a professional musician would earn him enough money to move to Spain and take guitar lessons from the legendary classical guitarist Andrés Segovia. "He did, though, think that if he was lucky, he could make enough money from six months of being a full-time pop musician, that he could move to Spain and take guitar lessons from psychovia."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Child Psychologist (1950s)
podcast.body: Following his sister's sudden death, Ray became even more introverted, leading him to see a child psychologist. This was an "as far from the normal experience as it's possible to imagine" for a working-class child in the 1950s, highlighting the profound impact of his trauma. "For the next year, Ray was even more introverted than normal, to the point that he actually ended up seeing a child psychologist."

podcast.title: Cynical Motivation for Early Collaboration
podcast.body: Ray fostered closeness with his younger brother Dave due to a "cynical motive" related to their pocket money. Ray would advise Dave on "good new records," prompting Dave to buy them, which allowed Ray to play them while spending his own money on other things. "Dave would go out and buy them, and then Ray could play them and spend his own money on other things."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Difficult Sibling Relationship
podcast.body: Ray had a "difficult relationship" with his younger brother Dave, partly due to their "diametrically opposed personalities." Ray was described as "introverted, thoughtful, and notoriously selfish," and as the former youngest child and only boy, he "resented" Dave taking attention he considered his by right. "Ray was introverted, thoughtful, and notoriously selfish... Ray... resented his younger brother coming along and taking the attention he saw as his by right."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dislike of Original "You Really Got Me" Recording
podcast.body: Ray Davis was "devastated" by Shell Tauhmey's initial overproduced recording of "You Really Got Me," which he felt was a "Phil Spector sound-alike" drenched in echo, and did not want it released. He, along with Dave, described it as being taken "much slower." "Ray in particular was devastated by the result, and didn't want it released."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Disputed Session Guitarist Credit (Jimmy Page)
podcast.body: It has been reported by various sources, notably producer Shell Tauhmey, that session guitarist Jimmy Page played Ray Davis's rhythm parts on most of The Kinks' early recordings. However, this claim is disputed by other sources, including Ray Davis himself, who "insisted he played the parts." "It's also been reported by various people, notably Shell Tommie, that the session guitar is Jimmy Page played Ray Davis's rhythm parts for him, and most of the groups early recordings, although other sources dispute that, including Ray himself, who insisted he played the parts."

podcast.title: Experimental Film Acting
podcast.body: During his time at Hornsey Art School, Ray Davis starred in several "now-lost experimental films" created by the individual who managed the college's film society, indicating his early artistic ventures beyond music. "Davis also starred in some now-lost experimental films, made by the person who ran the film's society."

podcast.title: Exploration of Gender and Sexuality
podcast.body: Ray Davis has "always been keen to play around with notions of gender and sexuality" in his work. This tendency contributed to manager Larry Page's decision to change a lyric in "You Really Got Me" from "yeah you really got me going" to "girl you really got me going," partly to address subtle questions about the group's sexuality. "Ray has always been keen to play around with notions of gender and sexuality."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Hornsey Art School Experience
podcast.body: After leaving school, Ray attended Hornsey Art School, where he felt completely "in his element." Despite his working-class background, Ray harbored a desire to "climb the social ladder" and thrived among people interested in art and music. His particular passion at the time was cinema, regularly attending college film society showings of works by directors such as Bergman, Kurosawa, Truffaut, Eisenstein, and Griffith, although he would complain about the one-shilling entry fee. "Ray, on the other hand, was in his element. While Ray grew up on a council estate and was thoroughly working class, he had always had a tendency to want to climb the social ladder, and he was delighted to be surrounded by people who were interested in art and music."

podcast.title: Influenced by Tommy Steele's Style
podcast.body: Ray Davies's musical style, particularly his "cockney archness," is noted as an evolution of the "overly manored, musical inspired, cocknified impression of an American singing style" pioneered by Tommy Steele. "as we can also hear a style that will be taken up by ... Ray Davis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Return to Brother's Band
podcast.body: After spending time learning from jazz musicians in the Dave Hunt Rhythm and Blues band, Ray ultimately decided to rejoin his brother Dave's group. This decision was notably influenced by Dave playing him Civil Davis's "Country Line Special," which Ray saw as a bridge between the music he was playing and his desired sound, described as "Big Bill Broonzy with drums." "Ray later remembered that the thing that swung it for him was when Dave played him a record by civil Davis, country line special, which he thought of as a bridge between the kind of music he was playing with Dave Hunt, and the kind of music he wanted to be playing, which he described as big build runesy with drums."

podcast.title: Sister's Death and First Guitar (1950s)
podcast.body: Ray's sister, Really, gave him his first guitar as a 13th birthday present, after he had been asking his parents for one for nearly a year since Elvis became popular. That same night, Really, who had a heart condition from childhood rheumatic fever and was advised to avoid exercise but loved dancing, died at a dance hall at age 31. This traumatic event, where his last memory of her was receiving the guitar, deepened his introversion and led him to believe he was "intended by faith to play the guitar." "The last time Ray ever saw his sister was when she was giving him his guitar."

podcast.title: Songwriting Mentorship by Larry Page
podcast.body: Larry Page actively worked with Ray Davis, focusing on teaching him the "craft of songwriting." Page had a clear philosophy that hit songs needed to connect with the audience, specifically advising the brothers to write songs with "I, me, and you in the title, and repeat those words as much as possible." "Page was working hard with Ray, who was the brother who was Morrie get to learn the craft of songwriting."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Temporary Membership in Dave Hunt Rhythm and Blues band
podcast.body: Ray joined the Dave Hunt Rhythm and Blues band after being offered an audition by Giorgio Gomelsky. While with this group, he played Trad and blues music, including pieces like "Honky Tonk Train Blues" in the style of Bob Crosby's Bobcats. This period offered him "more prestigious gigs" and he learned from jazz musicians, temporarily causing the Ray Davis Quartet to seem "over." "for a while it looked like the Ray Davis Quartet were over, as Ray was getting more prestigious gigs with the Dave Hunt group."
